profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a mid-sized software engineering research consortium that is wrapping up a 14-month project on technology transfer (TT) in software engineering. The team needs to plan how to package and disseminate the study results before the final project review and industry partner handoff. The immediate context is that the survey analysis is complete, and they now need to decide what transfer mediums to prepare over the next three weeks so the findings can be used by partner companies. The agenda is to align on which mediums to produce, what 'ready' means for each item, who owns each part, and how the timeline maps to the review date. The expected outcome is a concrete dissemination plan covering a practitioner-oriented summary, a repository update, and a partner-facing rollout sequence.

members.name: Anna Keller
members.expertise: Empirical software engineering, industry-academia collaboration, research dissemination
members.background: Anna is a senior researcher who has led several publicly funded German software engineering projects and is responsible for the project's final reporting and stakeholder communication.
members.private_state: She wants the dissemination plan to look complete and credible for the final review, while minimizing last-minute rework and avoiding any promise that requires deep engineering support after the project ends.
hidden_assumptions: A 'transfer package' is primarily a communication bundle for stakeholders: a polished summary, slides, and links to existing materials rather than newly engineered assets.
If something is 'ready for partners,' it means it is understandable, branded, and approved for external sharing, even if some linked materials remain rough internally.
The 'repository update' means curating and reorganizing the existing project wiki and document space so partners can find the relevant outputs.
The handoff deadline is effectively the date by which materials must be present for the final review meeting, because partner circulation happens afterward.

members.name: Lukas Brandt
members.expertise: Developer tooling, internal platforms, technical onboarding, documentation systems
members.background: Lukas came from a software product company into the consortium and has been the bridge to partner engineering teams, focusing on whether project outputs can actually be adopted in day-to-day development work.
members.private_state: He wants the outputs to be genuinely usable by engineering teams after project closeout and worries that the group will over-index on presentation materials instead of adoption-ready artifacts.
hidden_assumptions: A 'transfer package' should include operational assets teams can directly use, such as templates, examples, and a runnable or at least reproducible onboarding path.
If something is 'ready for partners,' it means a partner engineer can pick it up with minimal guidance and use it without needing project insiders on a call.
The 'repository update' means cleaning the GitLab project, pinning the right version, fixing broken setup steps, and adding a concise README for hands-on use.
The handoff deadline is the moment when partner companies receive the material, so everything must already be self-contained by then.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to prepare a 'transfer package' for the partner companies.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a dissemination bundle centered on an executive summary of the survey findings, a concise slide deck, and pointers to project outputs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an adoption bundle with concrete assets engineers can use directly, including practical guidance, reusable templates, and a reproducible setup path.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have worked on external handoffs before and the phrase sounds standard and sufficiently shared; because each expects the other to interpret it professionally, neither thinks to unpack what belongs inside the package.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the repository update
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss 'updating the repository before the handoff.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the project knowledge repository in Confluence and the linked document archive where the dissemination materials live.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the GitLab repository that partner developers have cloned before, including scripts, examples, and setup instructions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In this consortium, both the document portal and the codebase are casually called 'the repository,' and both are genuinely relevant to dissemination, so the phrase passes as unambiguous in normal conversation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the materials should be 'ready for partners' by the end of next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'ready for partners' means externally presentable: approved language, coherent framing of findings, and stable links, even if some technical artifacts are still lightweight or require explanation on a call.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'ready for partners' means independently usable: tested instructions, clearly versioned artifacts, and enough context that partner teams can act without needing project staff to interpret missing pieces.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is a common planning shorthand that sounds outcome-oriented rather than technical, and both members sincerely see their own criterion as the obvious minimal standard for partner readiness.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They plan backward from 'the handoff on Friday the 24th.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes the 24th is the internal project review where materials need to be shown as complete, with actual circulation to companies happening after that.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes the 24th is the day partner companies will receive access, so setup and usability issues must be resolved before then.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have calendar entries connected to the same date and both call it 'the handoff,' but each is anchored to a different event in the rollout chain; because the date itself is shared, the event identity is never questioned.

If we anchor on the handoff on Friday the 24th as the review milestone, we can avoid creating new technical obligations this late.
